opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so at Georgetown I was working in Nathan Schneider's lab, which was very much a computational linguistics shop. We cared a lot about careful annotation schemes and about getting the linguistic representation right. A lot of my work there was on semantic annotation, things like how prepositions and case markers encode meaning across languages.

The experiment that stuck with me was a fairly simple comparison. We had this carefully built pipeline: you'd do tokenization, then a syntactic parse, then feed linguistically motivated features into a model that predicted semantic labels. Every stage was something a linguist could look at and say, "yes, that makes sense." Then we compared it against a pretrained language model that we just fine-tuned end to end on the same labels. The fine-tuned model was just better. It wasn't a huge margin on everything, but it won consistently, and it took a fraction of the engineering effort.

At first that was a bit deflating, honestly. You put all this thought into the structure, and a big model that's never seen your annotation guidelines picks up most of it from a few thousand examples. But it reframed things for me. The interesting question stopped being "how do I hand-build the right pipeline?" and became "what has this model already learned about language, and how is it representing it internally?" If it's predicting these semantic distinctions that well, something in there has to encode them.

That's really what pushed me toward interpretability. I didn't come away thinking linguistics was useless. The opposite, actually. The annotation schemes and the linguistic theory turned out to be really valuable as a lens for probing and understanding models. They just weren't the best way to build the system anymore. So the linguistics moved from being the engineering to being the measuring stick, and that's been the thread through a lot of what I've done since.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was a pretty humbling experience. When I got to Georgetown I was coming from this very traditional computational linguistics mindset, where you build a pipeline: tokenizer, POS tagger, dependency parser, then some semantic layer on top, and every stage has its own carefully designed representation and its own annotated data. I spent a long time working on semantic parsing in that paradigm, especially around things like adpositions and case marking, trying to get these fine-grained supersense labels right across languages.

And the thing that changed my view was watching how fragile all of that was once you moved even slightly away from the data you trained on. Every stage compounded the errors of the one before it. You'd spend months on a beautiful linguistically motivated annotation scheme, and then a pretrained language model with essentially no linguistic structure baked in would come along and match or beat the pipeline on the downstream task, often with a fraction of the engineering.

At first that felt like a loss, like the linguistics was being thrown away. But the way I came to see it is different. The specialized pipelines were trying to force the model to represent language the way we think about it as linguists. What the end-to-end models suggested is that the structure might still be there, just not where we were putting it. The syntax and the semantics show up implicitly, in the representations, and you can go find them rather than impose them.

So that experiment basically redirected me. Instead of asking "how do I build the right pipeline," I started asking "what pipeline, if any, has the model already built inside itself?" That's a big part of why I ended up doing interpretability work. The linguistics didn't become irrelevant. It became the thing you use to form hypotheses about what's going on inside the model, rather than the thing you hard-code into the architecture.

astra-6.text:
It made me more cautious about assuming that a specialized pipeline is necessarily the best way to solve a language problem. With semantic parsing, you’re trying to turn language into a structured representation, and a pipeline can make that process look very clean. But each stage introduces assumptions, and mistakes at one stage can constrain everything downstream.

The question for me became: which parts of that structure are actually helping, and which parts are just making the system more complicated? I wouldn’t take that as an argument against computational linguistics. It’s an argument for testing whether the linguistic structure you build into a system earns its place.

sol-6.1.text: I’d frame the issue as a trade-off between specialization and brittleness. A specialized pipeline can give you clear intermediate representations and make errors easier to diagnose. But each stage also introduces assumptions, and mistakes can propagate downstream. So the question is whether that structure earns its complexity: does it improve accuracy, make the system easier to understand, or help it generalize? I wouldn’t treat specialization itself as evidence that a system is better.
